tips.title: Two numbers to know exactly
tips.body: UK mains is an **ac supply** at about **230 V** with a frequency of **50 Hz**. Both figures are stated in the specification and both are asked for directly, so learn them as numbers, not as "about 200-odd volts".

tips.title: Brown, blue, green and yellow
tips.body: **Live is brown**, **neutral is blue**, **earth is green and yellow stripes**. The earth wire is the only one with two colours, which makes it the easy one to anchor the other two against.

tips.title: The earth wire normally carries nothing
tips.body: The earth wire sits at **0 V** and **only carries a current if there is a fault**. That is the whole point of it: in normal use it does nothing at all, and you notice it only when something has gone wrong.

tips.title: A switch does not make the live wire safe
tips.body: A **live wire may be dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open**. The switch breaks the circuit, but the live wire on the supply side is still at about 230 V relative to earth — so touching it still gives you a path to earth.

tips.title: Both power equations must be recalled
tips.body: **$P = VI$** and **$P = I^2R$** are both on the recall list, not the equation sheet. Use $P = VI$ when you know the pd and current, and $P = I^2R$ when you know the current and resistance.

why.matters:
Every socket in the house is the same supply: about 230 V, 50 Hz, alternating. The topic is the two sides of that. What it lets an appliance do, $P = VI$, and so how much current a kettle needs and how thick its cable must be. And what it can do to you.

Three wires, three colours, three jobs. Knowing which one is at 230 V relative to the ground you are standing on is the difference between a repair and a shock.

examples.title: Why the kettle's cable is thick and the charger's is thin
examples.body:
Everything on the mains gets the same 230 V, so what differs between appliances is the current, and $P = VI$ gives it: $I = P \div V$. A 2 070 W kettle draws $2 070 \div 230 = 9$ A. A 10 W phone charger draws about 0.04 A, more than two hundred times less.

A wire warms in proportion to the current through it, so the kettle needs a fat copper core to carry 9 A without heating, and the charger can make do with a thread. The fuse in each plug is chosen the same way: just above the current the appliance needs.

visual.alt: A table of a kettle, a toaster, a phone charger and an LED lamp on the two hundred and thirty volt mains, drawing nine amps, four amps, four hundredths of an amp and two hundredths

examples.title: Why the earth pin on a plug is the longest
examples.body:
Look at a UK plug. The top pin, the **earth**, is longer than the other two. That length is a rule from this topic, made in brass.

As the plug goes in, the earth pin connects first and, coming out, disconnects last. So the appliance's metal case is joined to earth before the live wire is ever connected, and stays joined until after the live has gone. If there is a fault inside, the case can never be live without a path to earth already in place. The long pin also opens the shutters over the other two holes, so nothing else can be pushed in.

examples.title: Why a bird on the power line is fine
examples.body:
A pigeon sits on a bare wire at thousands of volts and nothing happens. Both its feet are on the same wire, so there is no potential difference **across the bird**, and no pd means no current. The danger is never a high potential on its own; it is a **path from live to earth** through you.

A kite string or a ladder touching the wire makes that path, and the current follows it. The same rule at 230 V is why a live wire is dangerous even with the switch open: touch it while standing on the ground and you complete the circuit yourself.

steps.title: Direct and alternating potential difference
steps.body:
**There are two kinds of supply, and the difference is the direction of the current.**

**Direct potential difference (dc)** drives the current in **one direction only**. The potential difference has a **constant** value and a fixed polarity — one terminal is always positive. **Cells and batteries** supply dc.

**Alternating potential difference (ac)** **repeatedly changes direction**. The potential difference rises and falls and **reverses**, so the current flows first one way and then the other, over and over. **Mains electricity is an ac supply.**

**The UK domestic supply**, as the specification states it:

> Mains electricity is an ac supply. In the United Kingdom the domestic electricity supply has a **frequency of 50 Hz** and is about **230 V**.

Both numbers are examined directly, so learn them exactly.

**What 50 Hz means.** Frequency is the number of complete cycles each second, so the supply goes through **50 complete cycles every second** — reversing direction 100 times a second. Each cycle therefore lasts $1 \div 50 = $ **20 milliseconds**.

**On an oscilloscope** a dc supply gives a **flat horizontal line** — the pd is not changing. An ac supply gives a **wave** that rises above and falls below zero, crossing it twice each cycle.

steps.title: The three-core cable
steps.body:
**Most electrical appliances are connected to the mains using three-core cable.** The insulation covering each wire is **colour coded for easy identification**.

**Live wire — brown.** It **carries the alternating potential difference from the supply**. This is the dangerous one: it sits at about **230 V** relative to earth.

**Neutral wire — blue.** It **completes the circuit**, giving the current a return path. It is at, or close to, **earth potential (0 V)**.

**Earth wire — green and yellow stripes.** It is a **safety wire, to stop the appliance becoming live**. It is at **0 V**, and it **only carries a current if there is a fault**.

**The potentials are worth stating precisely**, because questions ask for them:

- between the **live wire and earth**: about **230 V**
- the **neutral** wire: at or close to **0 V**
- the **earth** wire: **0 V**

**Why the earth wire matters.** If a fault lets the live wire touch the metal case of an appliance, the case becomes **live** at 230 V — and anyone touching it provides a path to earth through their body. The earth wire gives that current a much easier route straight to earth instead, so the case cannot stay at a dangerous potential.

**Note what the colour coding is for.** The specification says it is **for easy identification** — so that anyone working on the wiring can tell at a glance which wire is which, rather than having to test.

steps.title: Why the live wire is dangerous
steps.body:
**The specification asks you to explain two specific dangers.**

**A live wire may be dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open.**

Opening a switch **breaks the circuit**, so no current flows and the appliance stops. But the live wire **on the supply side of the switch** is still connected to the mains, and so is still at about **230 V** relative to earth.

If you touch it, you complete a circuit **to earth through your own body** — and the switch, which is somewhere else entirely, does nothing to prevent that. This is why mains work is done with the supply isolated at the consumer unit, not merely switched off at the wall.

**The dangers of providing any connection between the live wire and earth.**

Because the live wire is at 230 V and earth is at **0 V**, there is a large potential difference between them. Any connection between the two gives current a path, and since that path may have **very low resistance**, the current can be **enormous** — remember $I = V \div R$, so a small resistance means a large current.

That causes two problems. A **large current through a person** is potentially fatal. A large current through the wiring causes severe **heating**, which can start a **fire**.

**This is also why the earth wire works.** It deliberately provides exactly such a connection **for the appliance's metal case** — a very low resistance path to earth. In a fault the huge current flows harmlessly down the earth wire rather than through anyone touching the case.

steps.title: Power, energy and the appliance
steps.body:
**Power relates the potential difference across a device to the current through it, and to the energy changes over time.** That last phrase is the one to hold on to: **power is energy transferred per second**.

**Why $P = VI$ makes sense.** Potential difference is the energy transferred per unit of charge, and current is the charge passing per second. Multiply them and you get **energy per second**, which is power. The equation is not an arbitrary fact but a statement of what the two quantities mean.

**Why $P = I^2R$ is useful.** Substituting $V = IR$ into $P = VI$ gives $P = (IR)I = I^2R$. It lets you find the power when the **resistance** is known rather than the pd — common for a heating element, where resistance is the quoted figure.

**The squaring matters more than it looks.** Because the current is **squared**, doubling the current gives **four times** the power. That is why a small increase in current produces a large increase in heating, and why cables are rated by current rather than by power.

**Comparing appliances.** A 2070 W kettle draws 9 A from the mains; a 920 W appliance draws only 4 A. Since both run at the same 230 V, the **more powerful appliance draws the larger current** — which is why high-power devices need thicker cable.

**A practical consequence.** A thicker cable has a **lower resistance**, so for the same current $P = I^2R$ gives **less power wasted as heat** in the cable itself. Using cable that is too thin for the current is a fire risk for exactly this reason.

visuals.alt: An equation card giving the two power equations and V equals I R, with the units of every quantity

check.solution: $P = I^2 R = 4^2 \times 10 = 16 \times 10 = $ **160 W**. Square the current **first**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Know the two numbers exactly**: about **230 V** and **50 Hz**. Both are stated in the specification and both are asked for as recall.

**Define ac by direction, not by size.** An alternating potential difference **repeatedly changes direction**; a direct one drives current **one way only**. Saying ac "changes" is too vague — a dc supply that is turned up also changes.

**Give each wire its own job.** Live **carries the alternating pd from the supply**; neutral **completes the circuit**; earth is **a safety wire to stop the appliance becoming live**. Three distinct jobs, and questions ask for them individually.

**Say that the earth wire carries current only during a fault.** It sits at **0 V** and does nothing in normal use. That is not a detail — it is the entire design, and it explains why a fault is noticed at all.

**Explain the switch danger properly.** The switch breaks the circuit, but the live wire on the **supply side** stays at about 230 V relative to earth, so touching it still completes a path **to earth through your body**. A switch is not isolation.

**Explain the live-to-earth danger with the equation.** There is a large pd between live (230 V) and earth (0 V). A connection between them may have **very low resistance**, and $I = V \div R$ then gives a **very large current** — dangerous through a person and enough to cause **heating and fire** in the wiring.

**Pick the power equation from what you were given.** $P = VI$ when you have pd and current; $P = I^2R$ when you have current and resistance. Both must be **recalled** — neither is on the sheet.

**Square the current before multiplying.** $4^2 \times 10 = 160$, not $(4 \times 10)^2 = 1600$. Because current is squared, **doubling the current quadruples the power**, which is why cables are rated by current.

**Know what this specification does not include.** There is **no mention of fuses or circuit breakers** anywhere in AQA 8463. The mains safety content is the **three wires** and the role of the **earth wire**, so that is what to revise.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Mains electricity is an ac supply.**
- UK domestic supply: about **230 V**, frequency **50 Hz**.
- **Direct (dc)**: current flows in **one direction only**; cells and batteries.
- **Alternating (ac)**: the potential difference **repeatedly changes direction**.
- Appliances connect with **three-core cable**, colour coded **for easy identification**.
- **Live — brown** — carries the alternating pd from the supply.
- **Neutral — blue** — completes the circuit; at or close to **0 V**.
- **Earth — green and yellow stripes** — a safety wire to stop the appliance becoming live.
- The earth wire is at **0 V** and **only carries current if there is a fault**.
- pd between **live and earth** is about **230 V**.
- A live wire is **dangerous even when a switch is open** — the supply side stays live.
- A live-to-earth connection gives a **large current**: danger to people, and **fire**.
- **$P = VI$** and **$P = I^2R$** — both must be **recalled**.
- Square the current **before** multiplying in $P = I^2R$.
- **Fuses and circuit breakers are not in this specification.**

questions.prompt: Describe the three wires in a mains cable, giving the colour and job of each, and explain how the earth wire protects a user from a faulty appliance.
questions.solution:
Most appliances are connected to the mains using **three-core cable**, with the insulation on each wire **colour coded for easy identification**.

The **live wire** is **brown**. It **carries the alternating potential difference from the supply**, and sits at about **230 V** relative to earth. It is the dangerous wire.

The **neutral wire** is **blue**. It **completes the circuit**, providing the return path for the current. It is at, or close to, earth potential — **0 V**.

The **earth wire** is **green and yellow stripes**. It is a **safety wire, whose purpose is to stop the appliance becoming live**. It is at **0 V**, and importantly it **only carries a current if there is a fault** — in normal use it does nothing at all.

**How earthing protects the user.** Consider an appliance with a metal case, such as a washing machine, in which a fault develops — the insulation fails, or a wire works loose, and the **live wire comes into contact with the metal case**.

Without an earth wire, the case would now be connected to the live wire and would therefore be at about **230 V**. Anyone touching it would be standing on the floor, which is at earth potential, so their body would provide a **path from 230 V to 0 V**. A current would flow **through them**, which can be fatal.

The earth wire prevents this by connecting the metal case directly to earth through a conductor of **very low resistance**. When the live wire touches the case, the current flows straight down the earth wire instead, because $I = V \div R$ means current overwhelmingly takes the lowest-resistance route — and that route is the thick copper earth wire rather than a person's body.

Two things follow. First, the case **cannot remain at a dangerous potential**, because it is held at 0 V by its connection to earth. Second, the current flowing in the fault is **very large**, precisely because the resistance of the path is so low — which is what makes the fault detectable rather than silent.

So the earth wire works not by blocking the fault but by **deliberately providing the very connection that would otherwise be dangerous**, on terms that keep it away from the user.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between direct and alternating potential difference, and explain why a live mains wire is dangerous even when a switch in the circuit is open.
questions.solution:
**Direct potential difference (dc)** drives the current in **one direction only**. The potential difference has a fixed polarity — one terminal stays positive — and the current does not reverse. **Cells and batteries** supply dc.

**Alternating potential difference (ac)** **repeatedly changes direction**. The potential difference rises, falls, and reverses, so the current flows first one way and then the other, over and over.

It is worth being precise here, because a common answer is that "ac means the voltage changes". A dc supply can change in **size** too — turning a variable supply up alters the pd without making it alternating. The defining feature of ac is the change of **direction**.

**Mains electricity is an ac supply.** In the United Kingdom the domestic supply is about **230 V** with a frequency of **50 Hz**, meaning it completes **50 full cycles every second**, so each cycle lasts 20 milliseconds. On an oscilloscope, dc gives a flat horizontal line while ac gives a wave crossing zero twice per cycle.

**Why an open switch does not make a live wire safe.** Opening a switch **breaks the circuit**. No complete path exists, so no current flows and the appliance stops working. That much is true, and it is why people assume a switched-off appliance is safe to work on.

What the switch does **not** do is disconnect the live wire from the **supply**. The section of live wire between the consumer unit and the switch remains connected to the mains, and therefore remains at about **230 V relative to earth**. Only the far side of the switch is dead.

**The danger follows from that potential difference.** Earth is at **0 V**, and a person standing on the floor is effectively connected to earth. If they touch the live conductor on the supply side, their body becomes a **path from 230 V to 0 V** — a complete circuit, even though the switch is open, because the circuit is completed **through them and the ground** rather than through the appliance.

Using $I = V \div R$, the size of that current depends on the resistance of the path. Skin resistance can be high when dry, but falls sharply when wet, and at 230 V the resulting current can easily be enough to be **fatal**.

This is why mains work must be done with the supply **isolated at the consumer unit**, not merely switched off at the wall. It is also why any connection between live and earth is dangerous in general: a large potential difference across a low resistance produces a very large current, which endangers people directly and causes enough **heating** in the wiring to start a fire.

criteria.text: Explains direct and alternating potential difference and gives the UK mains figures.
Explains what an open switch does and does not do.
Explains the danger using potential difference and current.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Direct potential difference (dc)** drives the current in **one direction only**. The potential difference has a fixed polarity — one terminal stays positive — and the current does not reverse. **Cells and batteries** supply dc.

**Alternating potential difference (ac)** **repeatedly changes direction**. The potential difference rises, falls, and reverses, so the current flows first one way and then the other, over and over.

It is worth being precise here, because a common answer is that "ac means the voltage changes". A dc supply can change in **size** too — turning a variable supply up alters the pd without making it alternating. The defining feature of ac is the change of **direction**.

**Mains electricity is an ac supply.** In the United Kingdom the domestic supply is about **230 V** with a frequency of **50 Hz**, meaning it completes **50 full cycles every second**, so each cycle lasts 20 milliseconds. On an oscilloscope, dc gives a flat horizontal line while ac gives a wave crossing zero twice per cycle.

**Why an open switch does not make a live wire safe.** Opening a switch **breaks the circuit**. No complete path exists, so no current flows and the appliance stops working. That much is true, and it is why people assume a switched-off appliance is safe to work on.

What the switch does **not** do is disconnect the live wire from the **supply**. The section of live wire between the consumer unit and the switch remains connected to the mains, and therefore remains at about **230 V relative to earth**. Only the far side of the switch is dead.

**The danger follows from that potential difference.** Earth is at **0 V**, and a person standing on the floor is effectively connected to earth. If they touch the live conductor on the supply side, their body becomes a **path from 230 V to 0 V** — a complete circuit, even though the switch is open, because the circuit is completed **through them and the ground** rather than through the appliance.

Using $I = V \div R$, the size of that current depends on the resistance of the path. Skin resistance can be high when dry, but falls sharply when wet, and at 230 V the resulting current can easily be enough to be **fatal**.

This is why mains work must be done with the supply **isolated at the consumer unit**, not merely switched off at the wall. It is also why any connection between live and earth is dangerous in general: a large potential difference across a low resistance produces a very large current, which endangers people directly and causes enough **heating** in the wiring to start a fire.

examTechnique.body:
Know the figures exactly: **about 230 V** at **50 Hz**, and that mains is **ac**. Define ac by the **change of direction**, not by size.

Give each wire its **own job**, and remember the earth wire carries current **only in a fault**. Pick the power equation that matches what you were given, and **square the current first** in $P = I^2R$.
examinerErrors: Giving the mains as 240 V rather than about 230 V.
Defining ac as "the voltage changes" without mentioning direction.
Swapping the live and neutral colours.
Saying the earth wire carries current all the time.
Claiming an open switch makes the live wire safe.
Multiplying before squaring in P = I²R.
Expecting the power equations to be on the equation sheet.
Writing about fuses, which are not in this specification.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer gives **230 V** and **50 Hz** exactly, and defines **ac by its change of direction** rather than by change of size. It gives each wire a **distinct job**, states that the earth wire sits at **0 V** and carries current **only in a fault**, and explains earthing as **deliberately providing a low-resistance path** so the current avoids the person. On the switch it separates what the switch does — breaks the circuit — from what it does not: disconnect the **supply side**, which stays at 230 V. It reaches for $I = V \div R$ to explain why a live-to-earth connection produces such a large current, and it **squares the current first** in $P = I^2R$, noting that doubling the current **quadruples** the power.
